pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; Dressing for the Weather (PROCEDURAL, 0.003): choose appropriate clothing/equipment for different weather — coat & umbrella for rain, sun hat & sunscreen for hot sun, warm layers for cold — understanding that weather affects what we do and how we prepare each day.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 weather observation (Y1 'Seasonal changes') applied to daily life; overlaps PSHE (looking after yourself, sun safety). State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS): applies K-ESS2-1 weather observation (VERIFIED verbatim) to a practical decision; connects to K-ESS3-2 preparing for weather. This is the everyday 'so what?' of observing the weather.
• Operational details — A simple cause→choice procedure: read/observe the weather → pick clothing/equipment that matches. Land that the CHOICE follows from the weather (rain→waterproof; hot sun→shade/cover/sunscreen; cold→insulating layers) and that weather shapes daily plans. Include a light 'why' (a coat keeps rain off; layers trap warmth; a hat/sunscreen protect from sun) without deep mechanism. Sun safety (hat + sunscreen in strong sun) is a worthwhile real-world habit. Prerequisites: Types of Weather + Temperature. Evidence: select appropriate clothing for ≥3 conditions; explain why certain clothes/equipment are needed; describe how weather affects daily activities.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/procedural): the child selects sensible clothing/equipment for at least three different weather conditions, explains why each choice suits the weather, and describes how weather changes what we do day to day — a practical, justified matching of preparation to conditions.
bestPractices: Frame it as a clear cause→choice routine: LOOK at the weather first, THEN choose — reinforcing that the clothing follows from the conditions.
Always attach a short reason to each choice ('a coat keeps the rain off', 'a hat shades your eyes and skin') so children justify, not just match — meeting the 'explain why' evidence target.
Cover the three core conditions (rain, hot sun, cold) plus wind, and include SUN SAFETY (hat + sunscreen) as a genuine health habit.
Introduce LAYERS for cold (several thin layers trap warmth; you can add/remove as it changes) rather than just 'a big coat'.
Connect to real daily decisions (walking to school, playtime, a trip) so the child sees weather shaping plans, not just outfits.
Use real weather/forecast input (today's actual weather) so the choice is authentic rather than hypothetical.
keyRepresentations: A dress-the-character surface: a weather scene + a wardrobe of clothing/equipment to drag on.
Weather→gear matching cards (rain→coat+umbrella; sun→hat+sunscreen; cold→hat+gloves+layers; wind→windproof).
A 'layers' build-up for cold (vest→jumper→coat) showing adjustable warmth.
Before/after outcome: dressed-right (comfortable) vs dressed-wrong (cold/wet/too hot) for the same weather.
commonMisconceptions: 'Coats/jumpers make heat' — they TRAP your body's warmth (insulation), they don't generate heat; keep this simple but don't imply clothes are heaters.
'Sunscreen/hats are only for the beach' — sun protection matters on any strong-sun day, not just holidays.
'Dress for the season, not the day' — a cold summer day or mild winter day needs dressing for TODAY'S weather.
'More clothes are always warmer' — overheating is possible; layers you can adjust beat one huge coat.
'You only prepare for bad weather' — hot sunny weather also needs preparation (water, shade, sun cover).

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, teach 'Dressing for the Weather' as a cause→choice routine: LOOK at today's weather first, THEN choose clothing/equipment that matches (rain→waterproofs; hot sun→hat, sunscreen, water, shade; cold→warm adjustable layers; wind→windproof). Each choice carries a short 'why' (a coat keeps rain off; layers trap body warmth; a hat and sunscreen protect skin), so children justify rather than only match. Centre a dress-a-character decision task where the child picks and then sees the comfort consequence, backed by matching/explanation checks and a real-outing performance task. Include sun safety as a genuine daily health habit, not just a beach activity.

activities.title: Dress the character, then see what happens
feedback: When the character is dressed wrong, show the felt consequence (soaked and shivering, or red and overheating) rather than only marking it wrong, then invite a retry.
When dressed right, confirm the comfortable outcome and echo the reason: 'The raincoat and umbrella kept the rain off — you stayed dry.'
For cold, highlight that several thin layers you can add or remove beat one huge coat, because you can adjust as the day changes.
If the child reaches for a coat on a hot-sunny day, ask how they'd feel running around in a thick coat in the sun, so the choice tracks the weather, not the routine.
activities.rationale: The topic is a practical decision the child should make and test; enacting a choice and seeing its consequence is intended to make 'look at the weather, then choose' a felt rule and to support the 'explain why' target. Draggable wardrobe items, comfort/outcome feedback, a stepwise layer build-up, and an optional live forecast are concrete interaction examples that may make the cause→choice loop visible; they are suggestions, not required mechanisms, and the loop's effectiveness is not independently validated here.
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1 weather observation applied to a daily decision; DCI ESS2.D weather = combination of sunlight, wind, snow/rain, temperature at a time/place.
learnerActions: Look at today's weather shown in a scene (ideally pull in the real local forecast so the decision matches the child's actual day).
Open a wardrobe of clothing/equipment (coat, umbrella, wellies, sun hat, sunscreen, water bottle, gloves, scarf, vest, jumper, t-shirt) and drag on what you think suits the weather.
Send the character outside and watch the outcome: in a t-shirt on a cool rainy day they come back dripping and shivering; with a raincoat and umbrella they splash about comfortably.
Switch to blazing sun: test good choices (sun hat, sunscreen, water bottle, t-shirt) versus a woolly jumper that leaves the character red and overheating.
Switch to a frosty morning: build up warm layers one at a time (vest → jumper → coat → gloves) and notice you can add or remove layers as conditions change.
For each round, say the little reason out loud ('the coat keeps the rain off', 'the hat shades my skin and eyes').
activities.intendedInsight: The clothing you choose follows from the weather you observe: look first, then choose, and each sensible choice has a reason tied to staying comfortable and safe.

activities.title: Get ready for real weather cards (performance task)
feedback: Target kits: hot-and-sunny → sun hat, sunscreen, t-shirt, water (not a heavy coat); cold-and-snowy → warm coat, gloves, scarf; rainy → umbrella and wellies/waterproofs.

If the child picks favourite or identical items across different cards, prompt the consequence: 'What will happen to you outside dressed like that in the snow?' to reconnect the choice to the weather.
If the child adds warm layers for hot sun, link clothing to comfort and safety: ask how they'd feel running in a thick coat in the sun.

If the child chooses nothing for strong sun ('it's nice out, I don't need anything'), introduce sun protection as active preparation: a hat and sunscreen are the hot-sun kit, just as a coat is the cold kit.
activities.rationale: Watching the child build the kit for each condition reveals whether they are matching clothing to weather or defaulting to habit/preference — something asking 'what do you wear in the rain?' would not expose as clearly. Acting out the choice and stating reasons meets the select-and-explain evidence targets across at least three conditions.
sourceClaims: K-ESS2-1 weather observation applied to a daily decision; DCI ESS2.D weather = combination of sunlight, wind, snow/rain, temperature at a time/place.
learnerActions: Lay out a mix of real or pictured clothing and equipment: sun hat, sunscreen, warm coat, gloves, scarf, umbrella, wellies, t-shirt, water bottle.
Draw three weather cards: hot-and-sunny, cold-and-snowy, rainy.
For each card, get a doll (or yourself) ready to go outside by choosing the right items, and act it out (e.g. actually put the coat on for the cold card).
Say why each item suits that weather.
Link it to the day: 'How does this weather change what we can do at playtime or walking to school?'
activities.intendedInsight: A child who can assemble a sensible, condition-matched kit for several different conditions — and explain the choices — has connected weather observation to everyday preparation.

activities.title: Match weather to gear and say why
feedback: Accept any reason that tracks the weather: 'the umbrella keeps the rain off me', 'the hat shades my eyes and skin'.
If a reason is missing, prompt for it — matching without a reason only meets half the goal.
Reinforce sun protection as a real answer for the hot-sun case, not an optional extra.
activities.rationale: A quick matching-and-explanation check confirms the evidence targets and is fast to run. On its own it illustrates and checks the pairings rather than giving the enact-and-see-the-consequence experience, so it is best used alongside the decision task.
learnerActions: Match each weather to its gear: rain → coat + umbrella; hot sun → sun hat + sunscreen; cold → hat + gloves + layers; wind → windproof.
For each match, answer a 'why do we wear this?' question in your own words.
Try a choice question such as 'What should you wear on a hot sunny day, and why not a woolly jumper?'
activities.intendedInsight: Children can pair conditions with appropriate gear and give a short reason for each pairing.

activities.title: Talk it through: why this, not that?
feedback: Draw out the reason, not just the item: if the child names a coat, ask what the coat does for them.
If the child says sun needs no preparation, gently surface overheating and sunburn as reasons to prepare for strong sun too.
activities.rationale: Prompting the child to justify choices directly supports the 'explain why' target. A straightforward procedural choice does not require open dialogue, so this is an optional complement for eliciting reasoning, not a stand-alone teacher of the procedure.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'It's raining out — what should I wear, and why?'
Explain why the umbrella is needed on the rainy day, and why a sun hat and sunscreen are the main things to choose on the sunny day.
Say what could happen on a hot, sunny day if you went out with no hat and no sunscreen.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the reasons into words strengthens the justification behind each clothing choice.

activities.title: Reference: dressed right for each weather
feedback: Point to the contrast: the same weather, two outcomes, because of the clothing choice.
Encourage the child to then make and test their own choice rather than stopping at the reference.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference illustrates the target and can scaffold a child who needs a model. Because the objective is a decision the child makes and tests, this reference should lead into the decision task rather than replace it.
learnerActions: Browse a scene of correctly-dressed figures for each weather, revealing a short 'why' under each (e.g. a flap you tap or lift).
Compare a dressed-right (comfortable) figure with a dressed-wrong (cold/wet/too hot) figure for the same weather.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing a worked example of sensible clothing for each condition, with reasons, supports children who need a model before deciding themselves.

constraints: Keep the 'why' light and age-appropriate: a coat keeps rain off, layers trap your body's warmth, a hat and sunscreen protect your skin — no deep mechanism needed.
Address the key misconception directly: coats and jumpers do NOT make heat; they trap the warmth your body already produces (insulation). Never imply clothes are heaters.
Dress for TODAY'S weather, not just the season: a cold summer day or mild winter day still needs matching to the actual conditions.
More clothes are not always warmer — overheating is possible; adjustable layers beat one huge coat.
Treat hot sunny weather as something to prepare for too (hat, sunscreen, shade, water), not only cold and rain.
Sun protection is a daily health habit on any strong-sun day, not only at the beach or on holiday.
Sun safety means hat, sunscreen, shade and water; never ask a child to look at or judge the sun through a cover or to hold material up toward the sun.

Matching/explanation and reference activities check or illustrate the idea but do not, by themselves, give the make-a-choice-and-see-the-consequence experience; pair them with the decision or performance task.
Prerequisites: Types of Weather and Temperature.

Evidence to look for: selects appropriate clothing for at least three different conditions; explains why each choice suits the weather; describes how weather affects daily activities (playtime, walking to school, outings).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched this session. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two underlying claims are marked unverified in the source: NHS/cancer-charity sun-safety guidance, and the clothing-insulation / 'coats make heat' misconception (AAAS Project 2061 / misconception research). The insulation claim is scientifically standard but was not re-checked here; sourceClaims cite only the verified NGSS K-ESS2-1 claim.

The verified NGSS K-ESS2-1 claim is cited in Activities 1 and 2 only to support the observe→decide content principle those activities enact; it does NOT validate the proposed enactment-and-consequence efficacy, which is kept in proposed/intended wording.

Independent fresh review found no learner-facing conceptual errors: the sun-safety observation method is stated safely (never look at/judge the sun), insulation is framed as trapping body heat rather than generating it, and no categorical medium-superiority claims remain. The one text edit softened an intendedInsight that overstated reliability of a single matching check.

probeDeeper: You picked the umbrella for the rainy day — why not for the sunny day?
It's hot and sunny — what could happen if you went out with no hat and no sunscreen?
How does today's weather change what we can do at playtime?
assess.correctAnswer: Hot-and-sunny: sun hat, sunscreen, t-shirt (not a heavy coat). Cold-and-snowy: warm coat, gloves, scarf. Rainy: umbrella and wellies (waterproofs). The child assembles a sensible, condition-matched kit for each card and can act it out (e.g. actually puts the coat on for the cold card).

errorPatterns.pattern: Dresses by preference or habit, not by the weather
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the concept — prompt the consequence: 'what will happen to you outside dressed like that in the snow?' to reconnect the choice to the weather.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the same or favourite items across different weather cards, ignoring the condition

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-generalises 'coat = going outside' — adds warm layers even for hot sun
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link clothing to comfort and safety: ask how they'd feel running in the sun in a thick coat, so the choice tracks the weather not the routine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts the winter coat on for the hot-and-sunny card because you wear a coat to go out

errorPatterns.pattern: Misses sun as something to prepare for — 'it's nice out, I don't need anything'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce sun protection as active preparation, not just cold and rain: a hat and sunscreen are the hot-sun kit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses no hat or sunscreen for strong sun

responseLevels.gap: Picks items by preference or the same outfit for every card; can't match clothing to the weather.
responseLevels.full: Assembles appropriate kit for all three conditions, explains why each item suits that weather, links the weather to what they can do outside, and adapts to a new condition.
responseLevels.partial: Dresses correctly for the obvious cases (coat for cold, umbrella for rain) but misses sun protection or can't say why an item is needed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a mix of clothing and equipment (sun hat, sunscreen, warm coat, gloves, scarf, umbrella, wellies, t-shirt) and three weather cards: hot-and-sunny, cold-and-snowy, rainy. Ask them to get a doll (or themselves) ready to go outside for each card, choosing the right items. Watch what they pick for each condition rather than asking them to explain the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child actually build the right kit for each condition shows whether they connect weather to preparation. A child who grabs favourite items or the same outfit for every card reveals they aren't matching clothing to the weather — something asking 'what do you wear in the rain?' would not expose as clearly.

Sun safety (hat, sunscreen, shade, cover in strong sun) is a recommended child health habit, not only for holidays/beach.

sources.claim: Clothing insulates by trapping body heat (it does not generate heat); layering allows adjustable warmth — a common young-learner misconception is that 'coats make heat'.
